summary: Defines the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation attribute, which can accompany BGP updates to supply the information needed to create tunnels and their headers. It provides encodings for many tunnel types, along with procedures for choosing among alternatives.

plainLanguage.summary: Routes can come with instructions for the tunnel to use, like send it through a tube of this type with these labels.

subtitle: How a BGP route can carry the tunnel type, endpoint and header details a router needs to send traffic through a tunnel.

tldr.problem: A router that must tunnel packets to a BGP next hop needs to know which encapsulation to use and how to fill in its header fields. Configuring that by hand on every router for every next hop does not scale, and RFC 5512 had limits that kept it from being used.
tldr.mechanism: A BGP path attribute, the Tunnel Encapsulation attribute (type code 23), holds a set of TLVs. Each TLV describes one tunnel type, and its sub-TLVs give the egress endpoint, header values and hints for choosing between tunnels.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9012 obsoletes RFC 5512 and RFC 5566 and is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 9830, so check that document too.

today: RFC 9012 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5512 and RFC 5566 and updates RFC 5640. It is updated by RFC 9830. The RFC states that RFC 5512 was never deployed in production.

sections.title: Why Routes Need Tunnel Instructions
sections.content:
Suppose router R1 must forward a packet toward a destination whose BGP next hop is router R2, but the routers in between have no entries for the destination. This happens in a BGP-free core, or when the destination is an IPv4 address and the routers in the middle support only IPv6. R1 must then encapsulate the packet and send it through a tunnel to R2, for example using GRE, L2TPv3 or IP in IP.

To build that encapsulation header, R1 must know the protocol to use and how to fill in fields such as a session id, key or cookie. The RFC says it would not be desirable to configure every BGP speaker with this for every one of its next hops. Instead, a BGP speaker tells the others, in effect, "if you need to encapsulate packets to be sent to me, here is the information you need".

RFC 9012 replaces RFC 5512, which only allowed the attribute on updates of the Encapsulation SAFI (SAFI 7). That SAFI was never used and its reconfiguration cost discouraged use of the attribute. RFC 5512 also had no way to name a tunnel egress endpoint, no way to signal outer IP or UDP fields, and only one-octet sub-TLV lengths.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a packet has to travel through a stretch of road where nobody knows its final address. So it rides in a sealed tube, and the tube needs the right labels. This RFC lets a router tell others exactly how to label the tube.

sections.title: The Attribute, TLVs and Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Tunnel Encapsulation attribute is an optional transitive BGP path attribute with type code 23. It is a set of Type-Length-Value (TLV) encodings, and each TLV describes one tunnel type. A tunnel TLV has a 2-octet Tunnel Type, a 2-octet Length and a Value made of sub-TLVs.

Each sub-TLV has a 1-octet type, a length and a value. The length is 1 octet when the type is in the range 0 to 127, and 2 octets when the type is in the range 128 to 255. Types come from an IANA registry.

The order of TLVs has no significance. Several TLVs may name the same tunnel type, and each one describes a different tunnel. The attribute may be carried in updates with AFI/SAFI 1/1, 2/1, 1/4, 2/4, 1/128, 2/128 or 25/70 (EVPN). Other AFI/SAFIs are outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute is a box holding smaller envelopes. Each envelope describes one kind of tunnel, and inside it are little cards with details like where the tunnel ends.

sections.title: The Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV (type 6) gives the address of the router that will decapsulate the payload. It holds a Reserved subfield, a 2-octet Address Family and an Address (IPv4 or IPv6). An Address Family of 0 means the egress endpoint is the BGP next hop, and the Length is then 6. In the AFI/SAFIs listed above, each TLV MUST have exactly one such sub-TLV.

The Encapsulation sub-TLV (type 1) carries values for the tunnel's own header, and its layout depends on the tunnel type. The RFC defines it for VXLAN (type 8), NVGRE (type 9), L2TPv3 (type 1), GRE (type 2) and MPLS-in-GRE (type 11). VXLAN and NVGRE use a 12-octet value with a V bit (VN-ID present), an M bit (MAC address present), a 3-octet VN-ID and a 6-octet MAC address. L2TPv3 carries a Session ID and an optional cookie of 0 to 8 octets. GRE and MPLS-in-GRE carry a 4-octet GRE Key.

Other sub-TLVs cover the outer headers and tunnel choice:

  • DS Field (type 7): one octet for the Differentiated Services field of the outer IP header.
  • UDP Destination Port (type 8): a non-standard outer UDP port; zero is malformed.
  • Protocol Type (type 2): an Ethertype limiting which payloads may use the tunnel.
  • Color (type 4): an 8-octet Color Extended Community used to match routes to tunnels.
  • Embedded Label Handling (type 9): value 1 or 2, controlling what happens to the label embedded in the NLRI.
  • MPLS Label Stack (type 10): a label stack pushed first, with the topmost label first in the sequence.
  • Prefix-SID (type 11): carries a value of the BGP Prefix-SID attribute from RFC 8669.
sections.plainLanguage: Each little card answers one question: where does the tunnel end, what secret number goes on the label, which road marker to use, or which kind of cargo is allowed.

sections.title: Extended Communities and Compatibility
sections.content:
The Encapsulation Extended Community (type 0x03, subtype 0x0c) comes from RFC 5512. It names only a tunnel type, so it is equivalent to a "barebones" Tunnel TLV: one whose egress endpoint is the next hop and which has no other sub-TLVs. The RFC says it is used in a number of deployed applications. Where a tunnel could be encoded as a barebones TLV, it MUST be encoded with the extended community, though an implementation MUST still be able to process a barebones TLV.

The Color Extended Community (0x03, 0x0b) carries a 4-octet user-defined color value, and its 2-octet flags field must be zero. If a Router's MAC Extended Community conflicts with a MAC address in a VXLAN or NVGRE Encapsulation sub-TLV, the extended community wins.
sections.plainLanguage: There is also an older, shorter note that only names the kind of truck. It still works, so routers have to keep understanding it.

sections.title: Choosing and Using a Tunnel
sections.content:
A tunnel is feasible for a packet when the router supports the tunnel type, the tunnel can carry that packet, the egress endpoint address is reachable, and no local policy forbids it. If the update has at least one feasible tunnel, the router MUST send the packet through one of them. When several are feasible, local policy picks, possibly guided by Color and Protocol Type sub-TLVs. The packet is then encapsulated and forwarded toward the egress endpoint, and that route may itself have a Tunnel Encapsulation attribute, so tunnels can be stacked.

If a route has the attribute but no feasible tunnel, it MUST NOT be considered resolvable for the BGP decision process. For recursive next-hop resolution, if the route to the next hop carries the attribute, the packet MUST go through one of its tunnels. If a TLV there has Color sub-TLVs, the tunnel can be used only when the original route carries a matching Color Extended Community.

For VXLAN and NVGRE, the virtual network identifier in the header comes from the Encapsulation sub-TLV when its V bit is set, and otherwise from a configured value. On labeled address families, the Embedded Label Handling sub-TLV decides whether the label from the NLRI goes at the top of the MPLS stack in the payload or is ignored or copied into the identifier. If no value is available, the tunnel cannot be used.
sections.plainLanguage: A router looks at the list of tunnels offered, throws out the ones it cannot use, and picks one that works. If none works, it treats that route as not usable.

sections.title: Validation and Error Handling
sections.content:
If a TLV's last octet is not the last octet of its final sub-TLV, or the attribute has no valid TLVs or lacks the transitive bit, the treat-as-withdraw procedure of RFC 7606 applies. A TLV with an unknown tunnel type is skipped as if absent, but it MUST stay in the attribute if the route is propagated. Unrecognized sub-TLVs are handled the same way.

A malformed sub-TLV is generally treated as unrecognized. The exception is the Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV: if it is malformed, the whole TLV is ignored and removed before the route is distributed. It is malformed if its length is wrong, if the address is a non-forwardable special-purpose address, or if the address is shown not to belong to the AS that originated the route. An optional procedure in the RFC checks the last point using the route origin AS. A valid but unreachable address is not malformed.

Most sub-TLVs MUST NOT appear more than once per TLV, and later duplicates are disregarded. Protocol Type and Color may repeat.
sections.plainLanguage: If one card is smudged, the router ignores that card. But if the card saying where the tunnel ends is bad, the router throws out the whole envelope, because without a destination it is useless.

sections.title: Scope, Filtering and Security
sections.content:
The attribute MUST be used only within a well-defined scope, such as a set of ASes belonging to one administrative entity. A BGP speaker that understands it MUST be able to filter it on incoming and outgoing updates, and on each external BGP session that filtering MUST be enabled by default. The same applies to the Encapsulation Extended Community.

The security section warns that the attribute gives an attacker a new way to divert traffic, especially through the Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV, and the traffic could be tunneled to a distant target across intervening infrastructure. Consequences include hijacking of traffic and denial of service. The AS check in the RFC helps, but an attacker able to inject the sub-TLV could also craft an AS_PATH that passes it. The RFC also warns about mutually recursive tunnel dependencies and routing loops, and notes that tunnels reduce the usable MTU, which the signaling does not address.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel notes should only be trusted inside your own neighborhood. Otherwise a stranger could write a fake note and send your packages to the wrong place.

fields.desc: Total number of octets of the Value field.
